title: 06 — Design Patterns: GoF and Beyond
html:
06 — Design Patterns: GoF and Beyond

How to read this: a pattern is a named solution to a recurring problem in a context, plus its consequences. The name is the point — it lets a team discuss structure in one word. Memorising UML is worthless; recognising the problem shape is everything.

Every entry below: Problem → Structure → Example → When to use → When NOT to → Where it already exists in .NET/Angular.

0. Pattern selection map

flowchart TD
    A[What is the problem?] --> B[Object creation is complex,<br/>conditional, or expensive]
    A --> C[Objects need to be<br/>composed / adapted / wrapped]
    A --> D[Behaviour varies, or objects<br/>must communicate]

    B --> B1["Factory Method · Abstract Factory · Builder<br/>Prototype · Singleton · Object Pool"]
    C --> C1["Adapter · Decorator · Facade · Composite<br/>Proxy · Bridge · Flyweight"]
    D --> D1["Strategy · Observer · Command · State<br/>Template Method · Chain of Responsibility<br/>Mediator · Iterator · Visitor · Memento<br/>Interpreter"]

Quick discriminators people confuse:

Confusion Distinction
Strategy vs State Strategy: client picks the algorithm, states don't know each other. State: object transitions itself between states
Adapter vs Facade Adapter: makes an incompatible interface fit an expected one (1:1). Facade: simplifies a complex subsystem (1:many)
Decorator vs Proxy Decorator: adds behaviour, client chooses to wrap. Proxy: controls access, client usually unaware
Factory Method vs Abstract Factory Factory Method: one product, subclass decides. Abstract Factory: a family of related products
Builder vs Factory Builder: step-by-step construction of a complex object. Factory: one call, picks a type
Mediator vs Observer Mediator: central hub coordinates known colleagues. Observer: broadcast, publisher doesn't know subscribers
Template Method vs Strategy Template: inheritance, fixed skeleton with hooks. Strategy: composition, whole algorithm swapped

1. Creational patterns

1.1 Factory Method

Problem: a class must create objects but can't know the concrete type at compile time.

public interface IReportExporter { Task<Stream> ExportAsync(Report r, CancellationToken ct); }

public interface IReportExporterFactory { IReportExporter Create(ExportFormat format); }

public sealed class ReportExporterFactory(IServiceProvider sp) : IReportExporterFactory
{
    public IReportExporter Create(ExportFormat format) => format switch
    {
        ExportFormat.Pdf   => sp.GetRequiredService<PdfExporter>(),
        ExportFormat.Excel => sp.GetRequiredService<ExcelExporter>(),
        ExportFormat.Csv   => sp.GetRequiredService<CsvExporter>(),
        _ => throw new NotSupportedException($"Export format {format} is not supported.")
    };
}

Use when: the type depends on runtime input (config, user choice, message type); you want creation logic in one place. Don't use when: a DI container already resolves it, or there's exactly one type. In .NET, IServiceProvider + keyed services (.NET 8: [FromKeyedServices("pdf")]) often replace hand-written factories entirely. Already in the framework: ILoggerFactory, IHttpClientFactory, DbProviderFactory, Activator.CreateInstance.

1.2 Abstract Factory

Problem: create families of related objects that must be used together, without naming concrete classes.

public interface IPersistenceFactory      // one family per database vendor
{
    IConnectionProvider CreateConnection();
    IPagingDialect      CreatePagingDialect();
    IBulkCopier         CreateBulkCopier();
}
public sealed class SqlServerFactory  : IPersistenceFactory { /* SQL Server flavours */ }
public sealed class PostgresFactory   : IPersistenceFactory { /* Postgres flavours */ }

Use when: mixing implementations across the family would be wrong (a Postgres paging dialect on a SQL Server connection). Don't use when: the products aren't genuinely coupled — you just get ceremony.

1.3 Builder

Problem: an object with many optional parameters and/or a valid construction sequence.

public sealed class QueryBuilder
{
    private readonly List<string> _where = [];
    private readonly List<string> _order = [];
    private string _from = "";
    private int? _limit;

    public QueryBuilder From(string table) { _from = table; return this; }
    public QueryBuilder Where(string clause) { _where.Add(clause); return this; }
    public QueryBuilder OrderBy(string col, bool desc = false)
        { _order.Add(desc ? $"{col} DESC" : col); return this; }
    public QueryBuilder Limit(int n) { _limit = n; return this; }

    public string Build()
    {
        if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(_from))
            throw new InvalidOperationException("From() is required.");     // validate at Build
        var sb = new StringBuilder($"SELECT * FROM {_from}");
        if (_where.Count > 0) sb.Append(" WHERE ").AppendJoin(" AND ", _where);
        if (_order.Count > 0) sb.Append(" ORDER BY ").AppendJoin(", ", _order);
        if (_limit is { } n)  sb.Append($" LIMIT {n}");
        return sb.ToString();
    }
}

Use when: > ~4 constructor parameters, many optional; immutable result; step validation. Don't use when: C# named/optional arguments or an init-only record with object-initialiser syntax does the job:

var options = new PricingOptions { Timeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5), Retries = 3 };  // simpler

Already in the framework: StringBuilder, WebApplicationBuilder, HostBuilder, ResiliencePipelineBuilder, UriBuilder, EF Core's ModelBuilder. Fluent builders are also the standard shape for test data builders (new OrderBuilder().WithLine(...).Build()) — a genuinely high-value use.

1.4 Prototype

Problem: creating an object is expensive; copy an existing one instead.

public sealed record PricingModel(string Name, decimal[] Curve, IReadOnlyDictionary<string, decimal> Params)
{
    public PricingModel WithBump(decimal bps) =>
        this with { Curve = Curve.Select(p => p + bps / 10_000m).ToArray() };  // record `with` = clone+modify
}

⚠️ Shallow vs deep copy is the whole difficulty. record with is shallow — reference-type members are shared. For a deep copy, clone explicitly; serialization round-trip works but is slow and loses reference identity. Use when: expensive initialisation (loaded config, compiled regex/expression trees, warmed models), or scenario/what-if analysis on a base object.

1.5 Singleton

Problem: exactly one instance, globally reachable.

// If you must hand-roll it: Lazy<T> is thread-safe and lazy by default
public sealed class FeatureRegistry
{
    private static readonly Lazy<FeatureRegistry> _instance = new(() => new FeatureRegistry());
    public static FeatureRegistry Instance => _instance.Value;
    private FeatureRegistry() { }
}

⚠️ Prefer DI singleton lifetime instead (services.AddSingleton<IFeatureRegistry, FeatureRegistry>()). You get the single instance without the global static, and it stays testable and replaceable.

Why the classic Singleton is considered an anti-pattern:

  • Hidden dependency — nothing in a method signature says it uses it.
  • Untestable — you can't substitute it; state leaks between tests.
  • Global mutable state — thread-safety and ordering hazards.
  • Hard to retire — once 200 call sites use X.Instance, you can't change the lifetime.

Legitimate uses: genuinely process-wide, stateless-or-carefully-synchronised resources: logging infrastructure, a metrics registry, a connection pool, a compiled-expression cache.

⚠️ The captive dependency bug (very common in ASP.NET Core): injecting a Scoped service (e.g. DbContext) into a Singleton promotes it to singleton lifetime — a DbContext shared across requests and threads → corrupted change tracker, random InvalidOperationException. Fix: inject IServiceScopeFactory and create a scope per unit of work. ValidateScopes/ValidateOnBuild in development catches this.

1.6 Object Pool

Problem: object creation is expensive and objects are interchangeable. Use: DB connections (built into ADO.NET), large buffers (ArrayPool<byte>.Shared), StringBuilder (ObjectPool<StringBuilder> in Microsoft.Extensions.ObjectPool), threads (the thread pool), HTTP connections (SocketsHttpHandler). Don't use for cheap objects — the pool bookkeeping and the risk of leaked/dirty state outweigh a gen-0 allocation, which in .NET costs ~a pointer bump. ⚠️ Must reset state on return or you leak one caller's data into another's — a real security bug class.

2. Structural patterns

2.1 Adapter

Problem: you need interface A; the thing you have offers interface B.

// Domain wants this
public interface INotificationSender { Task SendAsync(Notification n, CancellationToken ct); }

// Third-party SDK offers this
public sealed class TwilioClient { public void SendSms(string to, string body, string from) { } }

// Adapter
public sealed class TwilioSmsAdapter(TwilioClient client, IOptions<SmsOptions> options)
    : INotificationSender
{
    public Task SendAsync(Notification n, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        client.SendSms(n.Recipient, n.Body, options.Value.FromNumber);
        return Task.CompletedTask;
    }
}

Use when: integrating a third-party/legacy API, or keeping vendor types out of your domain (an anti-corruption layer — see file 07). Don't use when: you control both sides — just change the interface. In the wild: TextReader/StreamReader, IDataReader wrappers, Angular's HttpClient interceptor wrapping, ILogger adapters over Serilog/NLog.

2.2 Decorator

Problem: add responsibilities to an object dynamically without changing it or subclassing it.

flowchart LR
    C[Caller] --> L[LoggingDecorator]
    L --> Ca[CachingDecorator]
    Ca --> R[RetryDecorator]
    R --> S[SqlQuoteService<br/>the real thing]

public interface IQuoteService { Task<Quote> GetAsync(string symbol, CancellationToken ct); }

public sealed class CachingQuoteService(IQuoteService inner, IMemoryCache cache) : IQuoteService
{
    public async Task<Quote> GetAsync(string symbol, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        if (cache.TryGetValue(symbol, out Quote? cached) && cached is not null) return cached;
        var quote = await inner.GetAsync(symbol, ct);
        cache.Set(symbol, quote, TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30));
        return quote;
    }
}

public sealed class LoggingQuoteService(IQuoteService inner, ILogger<LoggingQuoteService> log) : IQuoteService
{
    public async Task<Quote> GetAsync(string symbol, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        var sw = Stopwatch.GetTimestamp();
        try
        {
            var q = await inner.GetAsync(symbol, ct);
            log.LogInformation("Quote {Symbol} retrieved in {ElapsedMs}ms",
                symbol, Stopwatch.GetElapsedTime(sw).TotalMilliseconds);
            return q;
        }
        catch (Exception ex)
        {
            log.LogError(ex, "Quote {Symbol} failed after {ElapsedMs}ms",
                symbol, Stopwatch.GetElapsedTime(sw).TotalMilliseconds);
            throw;
        }
    }
}

// Composition root — order matters: logging outermost sees cache hits too
services.AddSingleton<IQuoteService>(sp => new LoggingQuoteService(
    new CachingQuoteService(
        new SqlQuoteService(sp.GetRequiredService<IDbConnectionFactory>()),
        sp.GetRequiredService<IMemoryCache>()),
    sp.GetRequiredService<ILogger<LoggingQuoteService>>()));

Use when: cross-cutting concerns (caching, logging, retry, metrics, authorisation, validation) that should compose orthogonally. Don't use when: more than ~3 layers deep — stack traces and debugging become painful; consider a pipeline/middleware abstraction instead. In the wild: ASP.NET Core middleware, Stream decorators (GZipStream(new BufferedStream(fileStream))), Angular HttpInterceptor, MediatR behaviours, Polly pipelines.

2.3 Facade

Problem: a subsystem is complex; clients need a simple entry point.

// Hides: inventory reservation, payment authorisation, tax calc, shipment booking, email
public sealed class CheckoutFacade(
    IInventoryService inventory, IPaymentGateway payments,
    ITaxCalculator tax, IShippingService shipping, INotificationSender notifier)
{
    public async Task<OrderResult> CheckoutAsync(Cart cart, PaymentDetails pd, CancellationToken ct)
    { /* orchestrate the five, in the right order, with compensation */ }
}

Use when: you want to reduce coupling to a subsystem, or provide a coarse-grained API over fine-grained parts. ⚠️ Facades tend to grow into god objects. Keep them thin — pure orchestration, no business rules. If the facade starts making decisions, that logic belongs in the domain.

2.4 Proxy

Problem: control access to an object — for laziness, remoteness, protection, or caching.

Proxy type Purpose Real example
Virtual Defer expensive creation EF Core lazy-loading proxies, Lazy<T>
Remote Local stand-in for a remote object gRPC/WCF client stubs, HttpClient-backed API clients
Protection Access control Authorisation wrapper around a service
Caching Avoid repeated work (overlaps with Decorator)
Smart reference Extra bookkeeping (refcount, logging) —

Decorator vs Proxy: structurally identical. Intent differs: decorator adds behaviour the client asked for; proxy controls access and usually presents itself as the real thing.

2.5 Composite

Problem: treat individual objects and compositions of objects uniformly (part-whole hierarchies).

public interface IValidationRule { ValidationResult Validate(Order order); }

public sealed class AllOf(params IValidationRule[] rules) : IValidationRule   // the composite
{
    public ValidationResult Validate(Order order) =>
        rules.Select(r => r.Validate(order))
             .Aggregate(ValidationResult.Success, ValidationResult.Combine);
}
public sealed class HasLines : IValidationRule { public ValidationResult Validate(Order o) => ...; }

Use when: trees — file systems, UI component hierarchies, org charts, nested validation/permission rules, expression trees, menu structures. In the wild: Angular's component tree, Expression trees in LINQ, ILogger composite loggers, HTML DOM.

2.6 Bridge

Problem: two independent dimensions of variation would produce a class explosion (M×N classes).

Without bridge: PdfWindowsRenderer, PdfLinuxRenderer, HtmlWindowsRenderer, HtmlLinuxRenderer... (M×N)
With bridge:    Document (abstraction: Pdf, Html)  →  IRenderer (impl: Windows, Linux)  (M+N)

Use when: you can name two axes that vary independently (report format × output channel; notification type × delivery transport; shape × rendering API). Don't use when: only one axis actually varies — you've added indirection for nothing.

2.7 Flyweight

Problem: huge numbers of objects with shared intrinsic state blow up memory. Use: string interning, glyph caches, particle systems, tile maps, shared immutable config. In .NET: string.Intern, cached boxed values (bool, small ints are cached by the runtime), TimeZoneInfo instances, static readonly Money.Zero. Don't use unless you've measured a memory problem — it complicates lifetime and thread-safety.

3. Behavioural patterns

3.1 Strategy — the most useful pattern in business software

Problem: multiple interchangeable algorithms; the choice varies by context.

public interface IFeeStrategy { Money Calculate(Trade trade); }

public sealed class FlatFee(Money amount) : IFeeStrategy
{
    public Money Calculate(Trade t) => amount;
}
public sealed class TieredFee(IReadOnlyList<(decimal Threshold, decimal Rate)> tiers) : IFeeStrategy
{
    public Money Calculate(Trade t)
    {
        var rate = tiers.Last(x => t.Notional >= x.Threshold).Rate;   // tiers sorted ascending
        return new Money(t.Notional * rate, t.Currency);
    }
}

// Selection via keyed DI (.NET 8+) — no factory class needed
services.AddKeyedSingleton<IFeeStrategy, FlatFee>("flat");
services.AddKeyedSingleton<IFeeStrategy, TieredFee>("tiered");

Use when: the same decision point has several variants; you want to test each in isolation; variants come from config or plugins. Don't use when: there are two variants and there will always be two — a switch expression is clearer. In the wild: IComparer<T>, IEqualityComparer<T>, ASP.NET Core authorisation handlers, EF Core IModelCustomizer, RxJS operators.

3.2 Observer

Problem: many objects need to react to state changes in another, without it knowing about them.

// .NET idiomatic: events, IObservable<T>, or an in-process message bus
public sealed class OrderService
{
    public event EventHandler<OrderPlacedEventArgs>? OrderPlaced;
    private void RaisePlaced(Order o) => OrderPlaced?.Invoke(this, new OrderPlacedEventArgs(o));
}

⚠️ Memory leaks: an event handler holds a strong reference from publisher → subscriber. A long-lived publisher keeps short-lived subscribers alive forever. Always unsubscribe (-=, IDisposable, takeUntilDestroyed() in Angular). ⚠️ Ordering and failure: subscribers run in registration order on the publisher's thread; one throwing exception can prevent the rest from running. For anything important, use a real message bus with retries, not in-process events. In the wild: C# events, IObservable<T>/Rx, Angular EventEmitter/RxJS subjects, DOM events, INotifyPropertyChanged, domain events in DDD.

3.3 Command

Problem: encapsulate a request as an object → queue it, log it, undo it, retry it.

public interface ICommand { Task ExecuteAsync(CancellationToken ct); }
public interface IUndoableCommand : ICommand { Task UndoAsync(CancellationToken ct); }

public sealed class ApproveTradeCommand(TradeId id, UserId approver, ITradeRepo repo)
    : IUndoableCommand
{
    public Task ExecuteAsync(CancellationToken ct) => repo.SetStatusAsync(id, TradeStatus.Approved, approver, ct);
    public Task UndoAsync(CancellationToken ct)    => repo.SetStatusAsync(id, TradeStatus.Pending,  approver, ct);
}

Use when: undo/redo, transactional queues, macro recording, audit trails, deferred/scheduled execution, CQRS command handlers. In the wild: MediatR IRequest, ICommand in WPF/MAUI, job payloads in Hangfire/Quartz, Redux/NgRx actions.

3.4 Chain of Responsibility

Problem: pass a request along a chain until someone handles it (or all have processed it).

// ASP.NET Core middleware IS this pattern
app.Use(async (ctx, next) =>
{
    var correlationId = ctx.Request.Headers["X-Correlation-Id"].FirstOrDefault() ?? Guid.NewGuid().ToString();
    using (log.BeginScope(new Dictionary<string, object> { ["CorrelationId"] = correlationId }))
    {
        ctx.Response.Headers["X-Correlation-Id"] = correlationId;
        await next();                      // pass down the chain
    }
});

Use when: a request passes through ordered, optional stages: authentication → authorisation → validation → rate limiting → handler; escalation workflows; event filtering. In the wild: ASP.NET Core middleware, Angular HttpInterceptor chain, DelegatingHandler in HttpClient, MediatR pipeline behaviours, servlet filters, exception filters.

3.5 State

Problem: an object's behaviour changes with its internal state, and you have switch (state) in many methods.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Draft
    Draft --> Submitted: Submit()
    Submitted --> Approved: Approve()
    Submitted --> Rejected: Reject()
    Approved --> Settled: Settle()
    Rejected --> [*]
    Settled --> [*]

// Explicit transition table beats scattered ifs, and is easy to test exhaustively
private static readonly Dictionary<(TradeStatus From, TradeAction Action), TradeStatus> Transitions = new()
{
    [(TradeStatus.Draft,     TradeAction.Submit)]  = TradeStatus.Submitted,
    [(TradeStatus.Submitted, TradeAction.Approve)] = TradeStatus.Approved,
    [(TradeStatus.Submitted, TradeAction.Reject)]  = TradeStatus.Rejected,
    [(TradeStatus.Approved,  TradeAction.Settle)]  = TradeStatus.Settled,
};

public void Apply(TradeAction action)
{
    if (!Transitions.TryGetValue((Status, action), out var next))
        throw new InvalidOperationException($"Cannot {action} a trade in state {Status}.");
    Status = next;
}

Use when: ≥ 4 states with real behavioural differences, or when illegal transitions must be impossible. Don't build a state machine for a 2-state flag. In the wild: order/payment workflows, TCP connections, CI pipeline stages, circuit breakers (Closed/Open/HalfOpen), document approval.

3.6 Template Method

Problem: several algorithms share a skeleton but differ in steps.

public abstract class BatchImporter<T>
{
    public async Task<ImportResult> RunAsync(Stream input, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        var rows   = await ParseAsync(input, ct);            // varies
        var valid  = rows.Where(Validate).ToList();          // varies
        await PersistAsync(valid, ct);                       // varies
        await AuditAsync(valid.Count, rows.Count - valid.Count, ct);   // fixed
        return new ImportResult(valid.Count, rows.Count - valid.Count);
    }
    protected abstract Task<IReadOnlyList<T>> ParseAsync(Stream s, CancellationToken ct);
    protected abstract bool Validate(T row);
    protected abstract Task PersistAsync(IReadOnlyList<T> rows, CancellationToken ct);
    private Task AuditAsync(int ok, int failed, CancellationToken ct) => ...;
}

Use when: the skeleton is genuinely fixed and shared, and inheritance is acceptable. Prefer Strategy when: you want composition, runtime swapping, or to avoid a deep hierarchy. Template Method is the inheritance version; Strategy is the composition version. Modern .NET style leans Strategy or plain delegates. In the wild: BackgroundService.ExecuteAsync, ASP.NET Core ControllerBase filters, xUnit fixtures.

3.7 Mediator

Problem: N objects communicating directly → N² coupling. Route through a hub.

// MediatR — the de-facto .NET implementation
public sealed record ApproveTrade(TradeId Id, UserId Approver) : IRequest<Result>;

public sealed class ApproveTradeHandler(ITradeRepo repo, IPublisher publisher)
    : IRequestHandler<ApproveTrade, Result>
{
    public async Task<Result> Handle(ApproveTrade cmd, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        var trade = await repo.GetAsync(cmd.Id, ct) ?? return Result.NotFound();
        trade.Approve(cmd.Approver);
        await repo.SaveAsync(trade, ct);
        await publisher.Publish(new TradeApproved(cmd.Id), ct);
        return Result.Ok();
    }
}

Use when: you want thin controllers, uniform cross-cutting pipeline behaviours (validation, logging, transactions, caching) applied to every request, and clear one-handler-per-use-case structure. ⚠️ The honest counter-argument: mediator adds indirection. "Go to definition" on Send(new ApproveTrade(...)) doesn't reach the handler. For a small app, injecting ITradeService directly is simpler and more navigable. Adopt MediatR for the pipeline behaviours, not for the decoupling on its own. In the wild: MediatR, Angular services coordinating components, EventAggregator in Prism, Redux/NgRx store.

3.8 Iterator

Already ubiquitous: IEnumerable<T>/IEnumerator<T>, yield return, Python generators, JS iterators/generators.

// Lazy streaming — constant memory over an arbitrarily large file
public static IEnumerable<Trade> ReadTrades(string path)
{
    using var reader = new StreamReader(path);
    string? line;
    while ((line = reader.ReadLine()) is not null)
        yield return Trade.Parse(line);       // nothing is read until the caller iterates
}

⚠️ Deferred execution traps: the using above disposes only when enumeration completes or the enumerator is disposed — abandoning a foreach early still disposes (the compiler emits a finally), but capturing the IEnumerable and iterating twice re-reads the file. And IQueryable deferred execution is why .Where() in a loop generates N queries. IAsyncEnumerable<T> + await foreach is the async equivalent — use it for streaming DB reads and paged APIs.

3.9 Visitor

Problem: add new operations to a stable object hierarchy without modifying it. Use when: the set of types is stable but the set of operations grows (AST evaluation, compilers, serialisers, report generators over a document tree). Don't use when: types change often — you'd edit every visitor. (The "expression problem" trade-off again.) Modern alternative in C#: pattern matching over a sealed hierarchy gives you the same thing with far less ceremony and compiler exhaustiveness help:

static decimal Evaluate(Expr e) => e switch
{
    Literal l  => l.Value,
    Add a      => Evaluate(a.Left) + Evaluate(a.Right),
    Multiply m => Evaluate(m.Left) * Evaluate(m.Right),
    _ => throw new NotSupportedException($"Unknown expression {e.GetType().Name}")
};

In the wild: Roslyn CSharpSyntaxVisitor, ExpressionVisitor (LINQ providers — this is how EF Core translates your lambda into SQL).

3.10 Memento

Capture and restore state without exposing internals. Use for undo, snapshots, checkpointing, transaction rollback, event-sourcing snapshots. record + with gives you most of it cheaply.

3.11 Interpreter

Define a grammar and evaluate sentences in it. Use for rules engines, query languages, formula evaluation (a spreadsheet-like =A1*0.2), feature-flag targeting expressions. ⚠️ For anything non-trivial use a parser generator or an existing expression library — hand-written interpreters grow into unmaintainable grammars.

4. Modern / non-GoF patterns you actually use more often

4.1 Repository & Unit of Work

public interface ITradeRepository
{
    Task<Trade?> GetAsync(TradeId id, CancellationToken ct);
    Task<IReadOnlyList<Trade>> FindPendingAsync(DateOnly asOf, CancellationToken ct);   // intention-revealing
    void Add(Trade trade);
    void Remove(Trade trade);
}

Use when: you want the domain independent of persistence, or a test seam without a database. ⚠️ The debate: DbContext is already a Unit of Work and DbSet<T> is already a Repository. Wrapping EF Core in a generic IRepository<T> that exposes IQueryable<T> adds a layer that hides EF's capabilities and provides no real isolation. Recommendation: if you use a repository, make it task-based and specific (FindPendingAsync) rather than generic and query-leaking. If you don't need the swap or the seam, use DbContext directly and test with Testcontainers.

4.2 Specification

Encapsulate a query/business rule as a composable object.

public sealed class ActiveTradesSpec : Specification<Trade>
{
    public ActiveTradesSpec(DateOnly asOf)
        => Criteria = t => t.Status == TradeStatus.Approved && t.SettlementDate >= asOf;
}
// Composable: spec1.And(spec2).Or(spec3) — reusable across query and in-memory validation

Use when: the same business predicate is needed in multiple places (query filter + validation + authorisation).

4.3 Result / Either

public readonly record struct Result<T>
{
    private Result(T value)   { IsSuccess = true;  Value = value; Error = null; }
    private Result(Error err) { IsSuccess = false; Value = default; Error = err; }
    public bool IsSuccess { get; }
    public T? Value { get; }
    public Error? Error { get; }
    public static Result<T> Ok(T value) => new(value);
    public static Result<T> Fail(Error error) => new(error);
    public TOut Match<TOut>(Func<T, TOut> onOk, Func<Error, TOut> onErr) =>
        IsSuccess ? onOk(Value!) : onErr(Error!);
}

Use for expected failures. Makes the failure path visible in the signature so the caller must handle it. See file 05 §5.4 for exceptions-vs-result guidance.

4.4 Options pattern (.NET)

Strongly-typed, validated, hot-reloadable configuration. IOptions<T> (singleton snapshot), IOptionsSnapshot<T> (per scope, re-reads), IOptionsMonitor<T> (change notifications). Detail in file 16.

4.5 Middleware / pipeline

Chain of Responsibility applied to request processing. The mental model to internalise:

Request  →  M1 in  →  M2 in  →  M3 in  →  Endpoint
Response ←  M1 out ←  M2 out ←  M3 out  ←

Everything before await next() runs on the way in, everything after on the way out. Order is the entire configuration. Exception handler first, then HSTS/HTTPS redirect, static files, routing, CORS, authentication, authorisation, endpoints.

4.6 Null Object

Return a do-nothing implementation instead of null: NullLogger<T>.Instance, Stream.Null, an empty IEnumerable<T>. Removes null checks; don't use it when the absence is genuinely meaningful and should be handled.

4.7 Circuit Breaker / Retry / Bulkhead

Resilience patterns — full treatment in file 01 §11.

4.8 Dependency Injection & the Composition Root

The rule: all wiring happens in exactly one place (Program.cs), at startup. No new on a dependency inside business code, no service locator (sp.GetService<T>() scattered around) — that's just a Singleton with extra steps and hides the dependency graph.

Lifetime Instance per Use for Danger
Transient Every resolution Lightweight, stateful-per-use Expensive to create; disposables accumulate in the scope
Scoped Request (or explicit scope) DbContext, per-request context Captive dependency if injected into a singleton
Singleton Process Caches, config, HTTP clients, stateless services Must be thread-safe; never hold scoped services

5. Anti-patterns to recognise and name

Anti-pattern Symptom Fix
God object One class with 3000 lines and 40 dependencies Split by responsibility/actor
Anemic domain model Entities with only getters/setters, all logic in *Service Move behaviour to entities; or accept it for genuinely CRUD modules
Service locator container.Resolve<T>() in business code Constructor injection
Singleton abuse X.Instance everywhere DI singleton lifetime
Golden hammer Every problem gets microservices / a rules engine / MediatR Match tool to problem
Premature abstraction Interfaces with one impl, factories with one product, plugin frameworks with no plugins Delete; re-add at the second real need
Poltergeist Classes that only pass calls through Inline them
Magic strings/numbers if (status == 3) Enums, constants, typed IDs
Big ball of mud No discernible structure Modularise incrementally (strangler fig)
Lava flow Dead code nobody dares delete Instrument, prove it's unused, delete
Vendor lock-in by accident Vendor SDK types in domain signatures Anti-corruption layer / adapter
Distributed monolith Microservices that must deploy together Fix boundaries or merge back
Exception as control flow try { Parse } catch { default } in a loop TryParse, Result<T>

6. When to use a pattern at all

flowchart TD
    A[Tempted to apply a pattern] --> B{Do I have the problem<br/>the pattern solves, TODAY?}
    B -->|No| C[Don't. Write the simple code.<br/>Patterns are refactoring targets,<br/>not starting points.]
    B -->|Yes| D{Is there a language feature<br/>or framework facility<br/>that already does it?}
    D -->|Yes| E["Use it — DI container, records,<br/>pattern matching, LINQ, middleware"]
    D -->|No| F{Will a reader who knows the pattern<br/>understand this faster than<br/>the alternative?}
    F -->|Yes| G[Apply it. Name the class after<br/>the pattern so it's discoverable.]
    F -->|No| H[Simplest thing that works]

Three rules that keep pattern use honest:

  1. Patterns are discovered, not imposed. You usually refactor into a pattern when the third variation appears.
  2. Name things after the pattern when you use one (RetryDecorator, FeeStrategy) — the name is half the value.
  3. Modern language features replace many patterns. In C#: first-class functions replace many Strategy/Command cases; records replace Prototype/Memento boilerplate; pattern matching replaces Visitor; DI containers replace Factory/Singleton; IEnumerable/yield replaces Iterator. Knowing the pattern still matters — implementing it by hand often doesn't.

7. Interview angles

  • Explain Strategy vs State. Same structure, different intent: Strategy is chosen by the client and states are unaware of each other; State transitions itself and states know their successors.
  • Where is the Decorator pattern in .NET? Stream composition, ASP.NET Core middleware, DelegatingHandler, Polly, ILogger providers.
  • Why is Singleton an anti-pattern, and when is it not? Hidden dependencies + untestable global state; acceptable when the resource genuinely is process-wide and you express it as a DI singleton rather than a static.
  • How do you add caching to an existing service without changing it? Decorator registered in the composition root.
  • Design an extensible notification system. Strategy (per channel) + Factory/keyed DI (selection) + Decorator (retry/logging) + Observer or a queue (fan-out). Say which you'd actually build first — probably just an interface with two implementations.
  • When would you NOT use the Repository pattern? When DbContext already gives you UoW+repository and you're not swapping providers or avoiding a DB in tests; a leaky generic repository is a net loss.
